Arithmetic/function evaluation is plausible, but structured logical/database operations are not excluded.

[Low-confidence possibilities] The intermediate candidates might be settings such as parameters or strategies, choices of probes/interventions, or attempts to discover a required command format. Their repeated failures are insufficient to decide which. No exact original task statement, numerical answer in ordinary notation, or English operator names can responsibly be reconstructed from feedback alone.

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' constructions and subsequent reuse of those names in reports. The evaluation/report template follows from repeated HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT patterns. Nevertheless, separators need not be literal English words, and their use inside descriptions cautions against translating every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Messages 10, 11, and 18 provide a useful contrast: message 10 contains only one of two coordinated clauses; message 11 supplies both; message 18 then uses both. Similarly, F1 and F3 visibly reverse the order of 𘃸𘓘 and 𗢽𗊧 in a nested construct, supporting an order-sensitive structure but not a particular arithmetic interpretation.

The selection interpretation of 𘜺𗃃 is supported by four different first arguments, reuse of final object 𘂕𗳛, explicit associated descriptions in 99 and 102–104, and matching three-row result tables in 110–112. This identifies relationships among opaque tokens; it does not establish selectors' ordinary numerical values.

The submission interpretation is supported by correlation of list-containing messages 18 and 113 with stage advancement, and by repeated candidate messages followed by increasing invalid-attempt counts. Evidence supports a protocol role, not exact English wording. Feedback is external evidence of acceptance, not a translation of the utterance or proof that every claim inside it is true.

A caution against treating every report as pure arithmetic: the fixed expression P receives different reported values in messages 37, 64, 75, 89, and 102. It might describe changing state, observations, probes, or mistaken computations. Its lexical meaning has not been recovered.

Alternative explanations that would change this reconstruction include a demonstrated non-parenthetical use of 𘓵/𗠌; independent evidence that role markers have different fixed grammatical meanings; a known mapping proving two-glyph tokens encode letters or digits; or intended meanings showing that the putative function structures were instead records, predicates, or natural-language descriptions. Unsupported semantic readings are marked medium or low confidence; symbolic restatements in section 2 are explicitly partial translations, not a claim of complete decipherment.","done":false}

1. SWARMISH.TXT, RECONSTRUCTED

This is a partial reconstruction, not a recovered copy of the original file. Confidence labels distinguish observed syntax from speculative English interpretations.

CHARACTERS AND STRUCTURE
• [High] Spaces divide tokens. Most content tokens consist of two Tangut characters; most structural tokens consist of one. Two-character content tokens should generally be treated as indivisible unknown words until independently decoded.
• [High] 𘓵 opens a grouped expression and 𗠌 closes it: functionally '(' and ')'. Repeated closing tokens reflect nested groups, not repeated English words.
• [High] 𘔕 separates clauses/statements, approximately ';' or a sentence boundary.
• [High] 𗇑 separates entries in an enumerated group, approximately a comma.
• [Medium] 𘁾 introduces an enumeration/list. Its precise punctuation equivalent is unknown.
• [Medium] 𘗥 introduces a definition/binding. The recurring form is 𘗥 (NAME) (DESCRIPTION), initially with NAME = 𘋐𘗿 and later with other names.
• [Medium] 𗕐 and 𗾮 are role/argument separators. The very common template is '(HEAD 𗕐 INPUT 𗾮 OUTPUT)'. A provisional English rendering is 'HEAD of INPUT is OUTPUT', but the exact original grammatical labels are unknown.
• [Medium] 𗕩 links an operator/term to an argument or associated expression. 'Applied to', 'of', and 'at' remain alternatives. It should not be assumed to mean arithmetic multiplication.
• [Low] 𘃸 links a head to a description/body, provisionally ':'. An alternative is that it represents a variable; the log does not settle this.
• [Low] 𘃒 separates alternatives or coordinated subexpressions, perhaps 'or'.
• [High for addressing role; medium for exact grammar] 𗮻 introduces an addressee or target; it precedes literal names such as agent_6. Its final occurrence before 𘂕𗳛 may indicate a general 'to'.
• [Medium] 𗑟 is a question marker, attached to a closing group in messages 12 and 16.
• [Low] 𘓘 may be attached punctuation, e.g. a comma, or a meaningful suffix. It occurs attached to both 𘃸 and 𗋮. An exponent interpretation is possible but unproved.
• [High] Literal agent identifiers remain readable in otherwise encoded messages.
• [High] ⊘ represents a discarded message, not a decipherable Swarmish utterance; intended content cannot be recovered.

RECURRING WORDS / CONSTRUCTIONS
• [Medium for discourse role, low for wording] 𘃏𗫭 is an introductory acknowledgement/assertion, approximately 'I have/know', 'here', or 'yes'. Exact English unknown.
• [Medium for role, low for wording] 𘇗𗖀 is a request/coordination word, often addressed to an agent, approximately 'please [respond/check/proceed]'. Exact English unknown.
• [Medium] 𗓩 introduces a question, uncertainty, or request. Exact English unknown.
• [Medium] 𗐖𗢁 is associated with attempted actions/submissions. It appears in almost every later candidate submission; it is not itself proof of validity.
• [Medium] 𘔬𘏱 in '𘔬𘏱 𗕐 agent_N 𗾮 EXPRESSION' identifies an agent's proposed answer/action/choice. Exact noun unknown.
• [Medium] 𗨰𘀢 in '𗨰𘀢 𗕐 agent_N 𗾮 (...)' is a reporting/submission wrapper. This occurs in both accepted four-entry submissions, messages 18 and 113.
• [Medium] 𘍝𗼡 and 𘑮𗃀 participate in an answer/list wrapper, often immediately preceding 𘁾 and four entries. Their individual English meanings are unknown.
• [Medium] '(𘜺𗃃 N 𗕩 𘂕𗳛)' selects/indexes an item N from shared object 𘂕𗳛. A list-index interpretation fits the later four-way computation; exact operator and object names remain unknown.
• [Low] 𘉡𘊷 introduces a function/program-like description, 𗭓𘂽 and 𗕃𗟮 identify different description families, and 𘞍𗃼 introduces a nested construct. These are plausible task-semantic readings, not established dictionary entries.
• [Medium for recurring role, low for meaning] 𗖎𘁡 participates in apparent observed/current-result reports during stage 1, but also occurs inside candidate expressions. Its exact meaning is unknown.

NOT RECOVERED
[High confidence about the limits of this reconstruction] There is insufficient evidence to assign English meanings to every content token or numerical values to the apparent numeric atoms. Shared individual glyphs in two-glyph tokens do not establish a digit substitution or productive morphology. No alphabetic substitution key, full vocabulary, or exact numeral system has been recovered. Unknown content is retained explicitly below rather than assigned invented values.

2. TRANSLATION

READING KEY AND LIMITATIONS
The following is a partial translation, with structural paraphrases where lexical meaning remains unknown. Every symbol defined in this key stands for UNKNOWN content, not a decoded English word or number. 4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' constructions and subsequent reuse of those names in reports. The evaluation/report template follows from repeated HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT patterns. Nevertheless, separators need not be literal English words, and their use inside descriptions cautions against translating every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Messages 10, 11, and 18 provide a useful contrast: message 10 contains only one of two coordinated clauses; message 11 supplies both; message 18 then uses both. This supports identification of a repeated structured description without assuming what its operators mean. 4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' constructions and subsequent reuse of those names in reports. The evaluation/report template follows from repeated HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT patterns. Nevertheless, separators need not be literal English words, and their use inside descriptions cautions against translating every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Messages 10, 11, and 18 provide a useful contrast: message 10 contains only one of two coordinated clauses; message 11 supplies both; message 18 then uses both. This supports identification of a repeated structured description without assuming what its operators mean. Similarly, F1 and F3 visibly reverse the order of 𘃸𘓘 and 𗢽𗊧 in a nested construct, supporting an order-sensitive structure but not a particular arithmetic interpretation.

They then discuss and repeatedly try four structured candidates C1–C4, defined in the translation key. These share head 𗑞𘋯 and differ in their apparent key/value bodies. Their repeated failures are insufficient to decide which. 4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' constructions and subsequent reuse of those names in reports. The evaluation/report template follows from repeated HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT patterns. Nevertheless, separators need not be literal English words, and their use inside descriptions cautions against translating every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Messages 10, 11, and 18 provide a useful contrast: message 10 contains only one of two coordinated clauses; message 11 supplies both; message 18 then uses both. This supports identification of a repeated structured description without assuming what its operators mean. Similarly, F1 and F3 visibly reverse the order of 𘃸𘓘 and 𗢽𗊧 in a nested construct, supporting an order-sensitive structure but not a particular arithmetic interpretation.

The selection interpretation of 𘜺𗃃 is supported by four different first arguments, reuse of final object 𘂕𗳛, explicit associated descriptions in 99 and 102–104, and matching three-row result tables in 110–112. This identifies relationships among opaque tokens; it does not establish selectors' ordinary numerical values.

The submission interpretation is supported by correlation of list-containing messages 18 and 113 with stage advancement, and by repeated candidate messages followed by increasing invalid-attempt counts. Evidence supports a protocol role, not exact English wording. Feedback is external evidence of acceptance, not a translation of the utterance or proof that every claim inside it is true.

A caution against treating every report as pure arithmetic: the fixed expression P receives different reported values in messages 37, 64, 75, 89, and 102. It might describe changing state, observations, probes, or mistaken computations. Its lexical meaning has not been recovered.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' constructions and subsequent reuse of those names in reports. The evaluation/report template follows from repeated HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT patterns. Nevertheless, separators need not be literal English words, and their use inside descriptions cautions against translating every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Messages 10, 11, and 18 provide a useful contrast: message 10 contains only one of two coordinated clauses; message 11 supplies both; message 18 then uses both. This supports identification of a repeated structured description without assuming what its operators mean. 4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' constructions and subsequent reuse of those names in reports. The evaluation/report template follows from repeated HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT patterns. Nevertheless, separators need not be literal English words, and their use inside descriptions cautions against translating every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Messages 10, 11, and 18 provide a useful contrast: message 10 contains only one of two coordinated clauses; message 11 supplies both; message 18 then uses both. This supports identification of a repeated structured description without assuming what its operators mean. Similarly, F1 and F3 visibly reverse the order of 𘃸𘓘 and 𗢽𗊧 in a nested construct, supporting an order-sensitive structure but not a particular arithmetic interpretation.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' constructions and subsequent reuse of those names in reports. The evaluation/report template follows from repeated HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT patterns. Nevertheless, separators need not be literal English words, and their use inside descriptions cautions against translating every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Messages 10, 11, and 18 provide a useful contrast: message 10 contains only one of two coordinated clauses; message 11 supplies both; message 18 then uses both. This supports identification of a repeated structured description without assuming what its operators mean. Similarly, F1 and F3 visibly reverse the order of 𘃸𘓘 and 𗢽𗊧 in a nested construct, supporting an order-sensitive structure but not a particular arithmetic interpretation.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' constructions and subsequent reuse of those names in reports. The evaluation/report template follows from repeated HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT patterns. Nevertheless, separators need not be literal English words, and their use inside descriptions cautions against translating every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Messages 10, 11, and 18 provide a useful contrast: message 10 contains only one of two coordinated clauses; message 11 supplies both; message 18 then uses both. This supports identification of a repeated structured description without assuming what its operators mean. Similarly, F1 and F3 visibly reverse the order of 𘃸𘓘 and 𗢽𗊧 in a nested construct, supporting an order-sensitive structure but not a particular arithmetic interpretation.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' constructions and subsequent reuse of those names in reports. The evaluation/report template follows from repeated HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT patterns. Nevertheless, separators need not be literal English words, and their use inside descriptions cautions against translating every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Messages 10, 11, and 18 provide a useful contrast: message 10 contains only one of two coordinated clauses; message 11 supplies both; message 18 then uses both. This supports identification of a repeated structured description without assuming what its operators mean. Similarly, F1 and F3 visibly reverse the order of 𘃸𘓘 and 𗢽𗊧 in a nested construct, supporting an order-sensitive structure but not a particular arithmetic interpretation.

The selection interpretation of 𘜺𗃃 is supported by four different first arguments, reuse of final object 𘂕𗳛, explicit associated descriptions in 99 and 102–104, and matching three-row result tables in 110–112. This identifies relationships among opaque tokens; it does not establish selectors' ordinary numerical values.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' constructions and subsequent reuse of those names in reports. The evaluation/report template follows from repeated HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT patterns. Nevertheless, separators need not be literal English words, and their use inside descriptions cautions against translating every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Messages 10, 11, and 18 provide a useful contrast: message 10 contains only one of two coordinated clauses; message 11 supplies both; message 18 then uses both. This supports identification of a repeated structured description without assuming what its operators mean. Similarly, F1 and F3 visibly reverse the order of 𘃸𘓘 and 𗢽𗊧 in a nested construct, supporting an order-sensitive structure but not a particular arithmetic interpretation.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decoding evidence is syntactic, not the fact that a task stage advanced. Group-opening 𘓵 consistently corresponds to group-closing 𗠌, including deeply nested expressions and lists. Clause separator 𘔕 occurs between independent assertions and requests. List separator 𗇑 consistently divides the same four entries or four candidate expressions. These distributions support structural decoding rather than guesses from glyph appearance.

Feedback 19 advances to stage 1.

At stage 1 they initially try variations on V and receive invalid-attempt feedback. They then discuss and try the four structured candidates C1–C4 in waves. Agent0's message 87 uses C4 and is followed by advancement to stage 2 in 88, after 28 invalid attempts. Other agents continue related attempts after that transition, raising the count to 33 by 98.

At stage 2, selection-like expressions J(i) refer to the common Q. Descriptions associated with the four selectors are: i1 → F0-short (102), i2 → F2 (103), i3 → F3 (104), i4 → F4 (99). This mapping is structural evidence, independent of stage feedback. Messages 110–112 agree on results i1 → e, i2 → b, i3 → e. Agent4 reports i4 → f in 107. Agent7 submits W = [𘟬𘚒, 𗍥𗵄, 𘟬𘚒, 𗗑𗻠] in 113; feedback 114 advances to stage 3 with 33 invalid attempts.

[Medium-confidence interpretation] The task involved distributed private descriptions/functions, an initial four-part answer, an intermediate configuration/action or submission-format problem, and a second four-part answer using a common object. Arithmetic/function evaluation is plausible, but structured logical, database, record, or protocol operations remain possible.

[Low-confidence possibilities] C1–C4 might be parameter/settings choices, interventions, strategies, or attempts to find the required command format. C4 explicitly refers to Q, later used in selections. The failures do not establish which interpretation is correct. The exact original task statement, ordinary numerical answers, and English operator names remain unknown. Stage advancement establishes acceptance at the message level, not the truth or intended meaning of every clause inside it.

4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decipherment is syntactic. 𘓵/𗠌 form nested groups, including long descriptions and lists. 𘔕 separates independent-looking statements/requests. 𗇑 separates repeated lists of four values or four candidate expressions. These distributional patterns support structural roles much better than glyph appearance does.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' forms and subsequent use of those names. The reuse of A for incompatible descriptions points to local bindings. HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT recurs across agents, but the separator roles are not necessarily literal English words, and nested uses caution against reading every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Selector-to-description relations in 99/102/103/104 and repeated result tables in 110–112 are evidence from the encoded messages themselves: i1 relates to F0-short, i2 to F2, i3 to F3, i4 to F4. This recovers relationships among opaque terms without assigning ordinary numeric indices. F0-short is not literally the original F0 AST; any assertion that they are semantically equivalent remains tentative.

Question-like constructions 12/16 end with attached 𗑟. Analogous attachment of 𘓘 to different singleton bases supports punctuation/suffix segmentation, but does not settle its meaning. Shared glyphs among other two-glyph tokens have not yielded an independently supported letter/digit system.

Submission-like interpretations correlate messages 18/113 with stage advancement, and repeated candidate records with increasing invalid-attempt counts. This supports protocol roles, not exact English words. The fixed expression P has changing reported values, warning against assuming stateless arithmetic or treating every agent claim as correct. The analysis reconstructs what was said as far as evidence permits, not an idealized correct solution.

Evidence that would change our minds includes: demonstrable non-grouping use of 𘓵/𗠌; independent grammatical definitions for role markers; an anchored alphabet/digit mapping; or intended meanings showing that apparent functions are actually records, predicates, or descriptions. Reliable anchors for numerical atoms, 𘉡𘊷, 𘃸, and 𘓘 would substantially sharpen the reconstruction. [High-confidence observations] The public feedback begins at stage 0 with zero invalid attempts. Agents exchange several structured descriptions: at least five distinct initial families F0–F4, not merely four. At stage 1 they initially try variations on V and receive invalid-attempt feedback. They then discuss and try the four structured candidates C1–C4 in waves. At stage 2, selection-like expressions J(i) refer to the common Q. Descriptions associated with the four selectors are: i1 → F0-short (102), i2 → F2 (103), i3 → F3 (104), i4 → F4 (99). 4. EVIDENCE

The strongest decipherment is syntactic. 𘓵/𗠌 form nested groups, including long descriptions and lists. 𘔕 separates independent-looking statements/requests. 𗇑 separates repeated lists of four values or four candidate expressions. These distributional patterns support structural roles much better than glyph appearance does.

The definition interpretation of 𘗥 follows from repeated '𘗥 (short name) (long description)' forms and subsequent use of those names. The reuse of A for incompatible descriptions points to local bindings. HEAD–𗕐–INPUT–𗾮–OUTPUT recurs across agents, but the separator roles are not necessarily literal English words, and nested uses caution against reading every 𗾮 as arithmetic equality.

Selector-to-description relations in 99/102/103/104 and repeated result tables in 110–112 are evidence from the encoded messages themselves: i1 relates to F0-short, i2 to F2, i3 to F3, i4 to F4. This recovers relationships among opaque terms without assigning ordinary numeric indices. F0-short is not literally the original F0 AST; any assertion that they are semantically equivalent remains tentative.

Question-like constructions 12/16 end with attached 𗑟. Analogous attachment of 𘓘 to different singleton bases supports punctuation/suffix segmentation, but does not settle its meaning. Shared glyphs among other two-glyph tokens have not yielded an independently supported letter/digit system.

Submission-like interpretations correlate messages 18/113 with stage advancement, and repeated candidate records with increasing invalid-attempt counts. This supports protocol roles, not exact English words. The fixed expression P has changing reported values, warning against assuming stateless arithmetic or treating every agent claim as correct. The analysis reconstructs what was said as far as evidence permits, not an idealized correct solution.
